title: Following another school
hook: many scholars allow following another school's view in some cases

segments.voice: Yesterday, witr in many ways: one unit, or three, or more, joined or split, by school. Your line was odd, in any way. If you prayed witr last night, whose way did you pray it? Day one thousand two hundred twelve.

A question lands on a scholar's desk. A woman's husband left home and never came back. No letter. No word. No grave. Her family follows the Hanafi school, and in its classical books the answer is hard: she waits, for a very long time, before a judge may declare her free to marry again. The Maliki books give a judge room to act after a far shorter wait. So the scholar holding the question has two answers in front of him. One from his own school. One from a neighbor's. He can keep the door shut, or open it. Today: following another school.
screen: `A HUSBAND WHO NEVER CAME BACK.` → `TWO SCHOOLS, TWO ANSWERS.` → `KEEP THE DOOR SHUT, OR OPEN IT?`

segments.voice: Start with the ordinary case. A Muslim who isn't a jurist usually follows a school. Earlier in this block that had a name, taqlid: trusting a madhhab's method instead of rebuilding the law alone. So can a person step outside it? The jurists don't give one answer. Some held that once you take a school, you keep to it. Others allow following another school's view in some cases, and that's the line in today's index. Back to the missing husband. Hanafi scholars in South Asia, facing wives left in exactly that limbo, wrote a work that drew on the Maliki position, so a judge could end the marriage and the woman could go on with her life. The door was opened for a need, and through a judge, not on a whim. Some of those who allow it point to a line about fasting in the Qur'an, surah two, in Pickthall's words: "Allah desireth for you ease; He desireth not hardship for you." Then the warning on the other side of the door. The jurists have a phrase for picking whichever school's view is lightest, in matter after matter, just because it's lightest: tatabbu' ar-rukhas, chasing the concessions. Scholars who discuss the door also warn about this. And there's a related debate over talfiq, stitching: washing for prayer by one school's rule and praying by another's, so that the whole act might count in no single school. Some scholars forbid it. Some allow it within limits. Last, how it's actually done. A person with a real difficulty asks someone who knows both schools, and the answer comes with a reason. Not a hole knocked in the wall. A door, with a frame, that someone can tell you why to walk through.
screen: `TAQLID: KEEPING TO ONE SCHOOL.` · `A DOOR OPENED FOR A NEED.` · `NOT CHASING THE LIGHTEST VIEW.` · `ASK, AND HEAR THE REASON.` · then, large: `ALLAH DESIRETH FOR YOU EASE.`

segments.voice: The practice for today is to read about it, and that can wait until later. For now, sit, and let your breathing slow. Bring to mind a time someone made room for you: a deadline moved, a rule bent, an exception made because your situation really was hard. Who made that room, and what did they ask of you first? Then think of the other side: a time you asked for the easy way only because it was easy. Hold the two side by side. No need to judge either. Just notice the frame around the door. If you pray, you can ask for understanding in your own words. Later, if you want, look up what your school says about following another. The bell holds the time.
Following another school. Some scholars allow taking another school's view in some cases, for a real need, with a reason, and they warn against chasing whatever is lightest. Today's word.
Your line: doors between schools. Today, if you ask anyone for an exception, give them the real reason, and if someone asks you for one, listen for theirs. Day one thousand two hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Muslims who follow a school usually keep to its rulings, and when a hard case arises some ask a scholar whether another school's view may be followed; some scholars allow it for genuine need and warn against picking the easiest view each time.

fork.setup: you're a Hanafi scholar. a woman's husband vanished, and your school's classical books make her wait a very long time. what do you do?
options: tell her to keep waiting, whatever it costs her.
draw on the Maliki view, so a judge can free her.
tell her to pick whichever school she likes best.
fork.reveal: Hanafi scholars in South Asia drew on the Maliki position for these cases: a door opened for a real need, through a judge, with a reason.

original.note: Arabic: stitching pieces together; in law, combining different schools' views within one act.

trapdoor: what you thought: a school is a club, and stepping outside it is betrayal.
what it means: a school is a method, and some scholars allow taking another school's view for a real need.
what a scholar hears: taqlid, talfiq and tatabbu' ar-rukhas: following, stitching, and chasing concessions, each debated on its own terms.

notes: Editor pass: 'often point to' softened to 'some of those who allow it point to' (claims rule); practice and carry rewritten (exceptions made for a real need vs. the easy way) because 1207, 1209 and the old 1212 all asked who taught a rule and the reason behind it.
Previous ten days' scripts (1202–1211) were not on disk when this was written; the review was built from the index line for day 1211.
Index hook says 'many scholars allow'; the script says 'others allow' and 'some scholars allow' to keep within the claims rule. Keeper may confirm the stronger wording.

Missing husband (mafqud): classical Hanafi position (very long wait) vs. Maliki position (a far shorter wait, then a judge's ruling). Numbers deliberately left out. The South Asian Hanafi work drawing on the Maliki view is identified here as Thanawi's al-Hila al-Najiza; confirm attribution and framing.
Qur'an 2:185 is about the fast; the script says those who allow switching 'often point to' it as a general principle of ease. Confirm this is a fair description of how it is used.
Talfiq example (wudu by one school, prayer by another) and the summary 'some forbid, some allow within limits': confirm.
Original: تلفيق glossed as 'stitching'; confirm transliteration tal-FEEK and gloss.
